summary: Students build complete, equally-likely sample spaces (ordered lists or grids) for single and combined events, then compute theoretical probability as favourable ÷ total. They draw probability trees, multiply along a single path (AND), add across separate, mutually exclusive complete paths (OR), use the complement for 'at least one', and recompute second-level branches for without-replacement (dependent) events. The central hazard is assuming aggregated outcomes — such as the eleven dice totals — are equally likely, when it is the 36 ordered outcomes that are equally likely.
misconceptions: Assuming aggregated outcomes are equally likely — treating the eleven totals of two dice as each 1/11 (equiprobability bias)
Ignoring order when listing — counting 3+4 and 4+3 as one outcome, undercounting the sample space
Adding probabilities along a branch instead of multiplying (misapplying AND/OR)
Reusing the first-event probabilities on the second branch of a without-replacement (dependent) event

activities.title: The two-dice grid: why totals are not equally likely
steps: On paper or a 6×6 grid, write the total in every one of the 36 cells for (first die, second die), keeping the two dice as an ordered pair so 3+4 and 4+3 are separate cells.
Shade all cells where the total is 7 and count them (6 cells: 1+6, 2+5, 3+4, 4+3, 5+2, 6+1), then shade cells where the total is 2 (1 cell: 1+1).
Explain in a sentence why P(7) is NOT 1/11, referring to the 36 equally-likely ordered outcomes.
activities.insight: The 36 ordered (die1, die2) outcomes are equally likely; the eleven totals 2–12 are NOT, because different totals arise from different numbers of ordered outcomes.

activities.title: Trees: multiply along a path, add across paths
steps: Draw a probability tree for a coin flip followed by a die roll, writing the probability on each branch and checking each set of branches sums to 1.
Find P(tail and 6) by multiplying along the single path: 1/2 × 1/6 = 1/12.
Find a two-path 'OR' probability by computing each separate complete path's product, then adding the path products together (the paths are mutually exclusive, so adding is valid).
Leave fractions uncancelled until the final step so paths share common denominators when added.
activities.insight: Along one path, combined events use AND and you multiply; across separate complete paths that each satisfy the question, you use OR and add. These are different operations for different situations.

activities.title: Without replacement: the second branch changes
steps: Set up a bag problem, e.g. 3 red and 2 blue counters, and draw a tree for taking two counters without replacing the first.

Write the first-draw probabilities (3/5 red, 2/5 blue), then recompute each second-draw branch from the reduced situation — one fewer counter in total, and one fewer of whatever was drawn (e.g. after a red: 2/4 red, 2/4 blue).

If an optional tool offers a 'replace / don't replace' switch, toggle it and watch the second-level branch probabilities change (with no replacement) or stay the same (with replacement) to see the dependency.
Find a combined probability, e.g. P(two reds) = 3/5 × 2/4 = 6/20 = 3/10, multiplying along the path with the updated second branch.
activities.insight: For dependent (without-replacement) events, the second draw's probabilities depend on the first outcome, so they must be recomputed from the reduced contents rather than reused.

activities.title: Drill and check: rules and the equiprobability trap
steps: Answer a short-answer item: P(total = 7) with two dice — write the fraction and justify it, explaining why the common answer 1/11 is wrong.
Solve a without-replacement item where the second branch must be recomputed, and explain why it differs from the first.
Where available, tap grid cells to reveal their totals or tap a tree path to reveal its product, using these only to self-check after you have reasoned.
activities.insight: Quick recognition and fill-in checks can reinforce the AND/OR rules and resurface the equiprobability trap, but learners should reason first and use any reveal only to confirm; such items check and consolidate the procedures and do not by themselves build a full fresh sample space.

checkQuestion: Give the child paper and this task: 'Two fair dice are rolled and the two numbers are added together. Work out the probability the total is 7. Then work out the probability the total is 2.' (Set the task and WATCH — watch whether they treat all totals 2–12 as equally likely or systematically build the 36-outcome sample space, whether they respect order when counting the ways to make 7, and how they express and simplify the answers.)
checkAnswer: A correct performance: builds the sample space of 36 equally-likely ordered (die1, die2) outcomes — via a grid or systematic list — finds 6 ways to total 7 (1+6, 2+5, 3+4, 4+3, 5+2, 6+1) giving P(7) = 6/36 = 1/6, and 1 way to total 2 (1+1) giving P(2) = 1/36. The student recognises the 36 ordered outcomes are equally likely but the totals are not.
